question: Where should the project menu ('the book') live when you come back to resume work? Your confirmed vision says: open Claude Code anywhere, run the Resurrection Protocol as a command, and the menu appears right there in the terminal — pick a project and it continues. The research team instead designed a small local browser dashboard (a page at localhost:8820, opened in Chrome) that lists every project with its next-action line and can focus or launch the right cmux tab with one click. Both surfaces would show identical rows from the same registry; the terminal menu needs no server and matches your described flow exactly, while the browser page gives an always-glanceable dashboard without occupying a Claude session but adds a small local web server (with its own security hardening) to build and maintain.
options: A) Build the in-Claude terminal menu first; add the browser dashboard later only if the menu proves it earns it
B) Build only the browser dashboard (the research team's original design)
research_recommendation: Option A. The report favored the browser as 'the way in' for adoption, but it never evaluated an in-terminal menu (it wasn't asked to), and every load-bearing piece of evidence — one row per project, generated next-action line, focus-never-launch, red/amber facts — applies to either surface. Your confirmed vision names the in-Claude flow; it is also the smaller build with no web-security surface. The browser page remains a clean additive Phase 5.

question: Three safety-critical cmux behaviors are still untested, and testing them costs something: (1) When the close step tells cmux to close a workspace while a live Claude Code session is running in it, does cmux ask for confirmation or just kill it instantly? The safe-close feature's final step relies on this — the researchers called it 'the single highest-value remaining test' — and testing it means deliberately sacrificing one throwaway Claude session. (2) Does closing the LAST workspace in a cmux window close the whole window or quit cmux entirely? Testing may briefly close a window. (3) Do the new cmux 0.64 features (hibernation, auto-resume, description survival across restart) actually work as documented? Fully testing these likely requires restarting the cmux app, which interrupts your live sessions. Are you willing to spend a throwaway session and one controlled cmux restart now, before the build, to settle these?
options: A) Yes — run the full test battery now on throwaway workspaces plus one scheduled cmux restart at a convenient moment
B) Run only the non-disruptive tests now; do the sacrificial ones right before the close skill ships
C) Skip the disruptive tests; ship with conservative guards instead (never auto-close the last workspace; treat tab-close as unconfirmed until first real use)
research_recommendation: Option A. Every one of these behaviors sits directly under a safety promise the system will make you ('SAFE TO CLOSE THIS TAB'). The cost is one throwaway session and one restart you pick the timing of; the alternative is discovering the answer during a real close. The report ranks the live-Claude close test as the highest-value remaining test.

question: Your installed cmux (0.64.19) includes an AI auto-naming feature (automation.workspaceAutoNaming) that generates tab titles from your conversation content. It is documented but nobody has verified WHICH AI model or endpoint it sends conversation content to — the controlling setting (automation.autoNamingAgent: 'auto') is undocumented. Your cmux tabs regularly contain confidential OKOA deal work. Separately, the Resurrection system will already write meaningful tab titles and descriptions itself whenever it launches or updates a project (from your own close notes, locally), which makes auto-naming largely redundant for registry-managed tabs. Should auto-naming be enabled?
options: A) Leave it OFF until we identify exactly what model/endpoint it calls; revisit after that
B) Leave it OFF permanently — the registry writes titles anyway; don't spend time investigating
C) Enable it now and accept the unknown
research_recommendation: A or B — never C. The report explicitly flags 'verify what model automation.autoNamingAgent calls before enabling' as an OKOA confidentiality question, and the registry writing tab titles at launch makes auto-naming redundant for every tab the system manages. B is the zero-effort safe default; A only if you want AI titles on hand-opened tabs too.

question: cmux 0.64 ships 'Agent Hibernation' (terminal.agentHibernation, opt-in): it kills idle background agent processes to free RAM/CPU, then resumes them from saved session state when you next visit the tab. This directly targets the 'my Mac slows down / freezes' half of your problem, independently of closing tabs. However: it is documentation-claimed only (nobody has tested it on your machine), and it kills idle processes by design — which could interact in unknown ways with the always-running ACOS token-watcher daemons and the in-pane resume hooks that your Eternity continuation system depends on. Opt in?
options: A) Test it on a throwaway workspace first; opt in only after confirming the in-pane hooks still fire and Eternity still works on a hibernated-then-resumed tab
C) Stay off; rely on closing tabs alone for performance
research_recommendation: Option A. The report's own upgrade warning applies: the single biggest risk on the adopt side is the platform breaking the in-pane hook that actually carries your resumes (a known upstream regression class, #5427). Hibernation is worth having — it attacks the freeze problem your vision names — but only after the hook-firing check passes on a hibernated workspace.

question: How should the book get its initial contents? Option one: it starts empty and grows organically — each project auto-enrolls the first time you start a Claude session in it (any directory carrying a project marker: a .acos folder, a CLAUDE.md, or a memory/handoffs folder). Option two: seed it on day one by scanning for those markers — today that finds about 18 directories with handoff folders across 'Vibe Coding' and 'OKOA' (plus 42 directories Claude Code has ever run in, many of them junk or one-offs). Seeding gives the menu immediate day-one value covering everything, but requires one curation pass from you (roughly 10 minutes) to archive the entries that aren't real active projects — for example, the 'Vibe Coding' parent folder itself carries a stray memory/handoffs folder and would appear as a row, and several old handoff-bearing folders may be finished work.
options: A) Seed now with the scanner, then do one 10-minute curation pass to archive the dead rows
B) Organic growth only — the book starts empty and fills as you touch projects
research_recommendation: Option A. The rebuild/seed script must exist anyway (the report requires a proven rebuild path in v1, demonstrated at 16/16 rows from handoffs alone), your confirmed vision says the book 'lists every active project' — which organic growth can't deliver for weeks — and a one-time human curation pass is exactly the 'explicit enrollment, never naive scan' spirit: a directory is a project because you confirm it is, not because a process once ran there.
